name: Sapphire
physical: Kept nearby for comfort during stress
summary: Sapphire is the blue corundum of wisdom, loyalty and truth, the September birthstone and a royal gem cherished for centuries in jewelry and lore.
intro: Sapphire is corundum of any color except red, though when people say sapphire they usually mean the deep blue gem. The blue comes from traces of iron and titanium. At Mohs 9, sapphire is among the hardest and most durable of all gems, which is why it survives daily wear in rings so well. The most valued colors are cornflower blue from Kashmir and rich royal blue from Myanmar and Sri Lanka. Many stones are heated to improve color and clarity. Sapphire also forms star stones and a rainbow of fancy colors, including pink, yellow, and the rare padparadscha, so it is a whole family rather than a single hue.
history: The word sapphire comes from Latin and Greek terms that probably referred to lapis lazuli in ancient times, and later to the blue corundum we know. In medieval Europe, sapphire was the gem of clergy, symbolizing heaven and purity, and kings wore it to protect against envy and harm. Persian legend said that the sky was blue because it reflected a giant sapphire on which the world rested. Famous sapphires include the Star of India and the sapphire in the engagement ring of Princess Diana, now worn by Catherine, Princess of Wales. Sapphire is the September birthstone and the gem of the 5th and 45th anniversaries.
meaning: Sapphire is traditionally the stone of wisdom and loyalty. Crystal practitioners link it to the Third Eye and Throat chakras and use it to support clear thinking, honest speech, and a calm mind. It is considered a stone of integrity, encouraging those who wear it to speak truthfully and to honor their commitments. People often reach for sapphire when studying, making an important decision, or beginning a new career. It is also linked to inner peace and to the discipline of meditation. Its deep blue color is said to calm restlessness and reduce overthinking. Sapphire has long been connected with royalty and fidelity, which is why it appears in so many engagement rings.
howToUse: Wear sapphire in a ring or pendant to stay connected to its focus and loyalty. Raw or tumbled blue sapphire is more affordable and works well for meditation: hold it at the brow and breathe slowly. Place a stone on your desk for study or business meetings. In a grid, combine it with lapis lazuli and clear quartz for a wisdom layout. Gift a sapphire to celebrate a graduation, promotion, or anniversary. Keep a small one in your bag when you want to remain composed during stressful discussions.
care: Sapphire is extremely durable at Mohs 9 and is generally safe to rinse with soapy water and a soft brush. Ultrasonic cleaners are usually fine for untreated stones, but avoid them for fracture-filled material. Cleanse by running water, moonlight, sunlight, sound, or smoke. Sunlight does not fade it. Store separately from diamonds, which can scratch it. A hard knock along a cleavage-like parting can still chip it, so remove rings before rough work.
identify: Natural sapphire often shows rutile silk, color zoning, and fine inclusions. Synthetic sapphire is chemically identical but extremely clean and may show curved growth lines. Look-alikes include blue spinel, tanzanite, iolite, and blue glass. Heat treatment is nearly universal and widely accepted, but diffusion-treated stones with color only at the surface should be disclosed. Untreated stones command premium prices and should be backed by a lab report. Beware of glass-filled or dyed corundum sold at suspiciously low prices.

No. Sapphire is the gem name for any non-red corundum, so it appears in pink, yellow, green, orange, white, and even the rare padparadscha. Blue is simply the classic and most famous color.
